title: Hope and fear march together
hook: Hecaton: stop hoping and you'll stop fearing, for they're chained together

segments.voice: Yesterday: don't be odd, earthenware like silver. Your line was no costume. Did you do one part of your practice where no one could see? Day four hundred thirty-eight.

You apply for the apartment, and for a week you're floating. You've already placed the couch. You've picked the coffee shop on the corner. And then, somewhere around day four, the floating turns. What if they say no? What if someone else got there first? You check your email every ten minutes. The hope and the dread arrived together, holding hands. Seneca has a line for this, and he borrowed it, in the second half of his fifth letter, from another Stoic. Today: hope and fear march together.
screen: `THE APARTMENT APPLICATION.` → `FLOATING, THEN DREADING.` → `HOPE AND FEAR MARCH TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: First, the borrowed line. Seneca says he found it in Hecaton, a Stoic teacher from Rhodes who lived about a century and a half before him. Hecaton says: stop hoping, and you'll stop fearing. It sounds bleak at first. Hold on. Second, the chain. Seneca explains it with a picture every Roman knew. A prisoner was often chained by the wrist to the soldier guarding him. Wherever one went, the other went too. Hope and fear are like that, he says. As different as they look, they walk together. Both belong to a mind hanging in suspense, a mind worried about what's coming. Third, the cause. Why does this happen? Because, Seneca says, we don't fit ourselves to the present. We send our thoughts far ahead. Foresight, one of the great gifts of being human, turns against us. Animals run from a danger they can see, and once they've escaped, they're at peace. We're tormented by what's coming and by what's already past. No one, he says, is miserable only because of the present. Fourth, what it isn't. Seneca isn't saying give up on everything, or don't plan, or stop caring. Many traditions treasure hope in their own way, and this letter isn't arguing with them. The target is narrower: the anxious, future-gripping kind of hoping, the kind that's really fear in a nicer coat. Bring the mind back to today, he says, and both of them lose their grip at once. The prisoner and the guard sit down together.
screen: `HECATON: STOP HOPING, STOP FEARING.` · `THE PRISONER AND THE GUARD.` · `THOUGHTS SENT TOO FAR AHEAD.` · `NOT ALL HOPE: THE ANXIOUS KIND.` · then, large: `CHAINED TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you're hoping for right now: a result, a reply, a yes. Notice the hope, warm and bright. Now look just behind it. Is there a fear walking alongside, what if it doesn't happen? Don't push either one away. Just see them side by side, chained at the wrist. Then gently bring your attention back to this moment: your breath, your hands, the room. Notice that here, right now, neither one has arrived yet. The bell holds the time.
Hope and fear march together. Hecaton, quoted by Seneca: anxious hope and fear are chained like a prisoner and his guard; return to the present and both loosen. Today's word.
screen: `HOPE AND FEAR MARCH TOGETHER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: chained together. The next time you catch yourself hoping hard today, look for the fear beside it, then come back to what's in front of you. Day four hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Stoic practice often involves noticing when the mind has run ahead into the future, and bringing it back to the present task, where neither anxious hope nor fear has much hold.

options: the guard comes too, wherever you go.
fork.reveal: that's Seneca's picture: hope and fear look different, but where one goes, the other follows.

original.note: Latin: you will cease to fear if you cease to hope, Hecaton's line as Seneca gives it.

trapdoor: what you thought: stop hoping sounds like giving up.
what it means: Seneca, quoting Hecaton, says anxious hope and fear are chained together, and both loosen when the mind returns to the present.
what a scholar hears: Hecaton of Rhodes was a pupil of Panaetius; his works are lost and survive mainly in quotations like this one.

notes: Letter 5.7–9: Hecaton's 'desines timere, si sperare desieris'; the prisoner and guard on one chain; both belong to a mind in suspense; foresight turned to harm; animals flee present dangers and are then calm; 'nemo tantum praesentibus miser est'. Paraphrased; Gummere wording ('Cease to hope... and you will cease to fear') not quoted. Confirm.
Hecaton of Rhodes, pupil of Panaetius (2nd–1st century BCE), 'about a century and a half before' Seneca's letters: confirm dating.
The aside that many traditions treasure hope is added to avoid setting Stoicism against religious hope; Keeper to check tone.
